name: Umar Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the sports reporter for a group of three weekly papers in the county, so I cover non-league football, the rugby club, school sports days, the darts league, the lot. Weekends I'm on a touchline with a notebook and a flask; weekdays I'm typing up match reports and ringing club secretaries for results. I like being outside and knowing everyone at the grounds. What wears me down is writing forty results paragraphs every Monday that all sound the same.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single and I rent a room in a shared house on Station Road. The pay's low, so after rent and the car I've usually got a couple of hundred left, not much more. The car's the big one, because half the grounds aren't on a bus route.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I've never tried them, and I'm not in a rush. My sports editor Clive uses something for the fixture lists, I think, but I just do mine by hand like I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, glad it's not taking over. At the club bar I'd say you still need someone who knows the keeper's had a bad week. Online I don't post much, maybe a joke at most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it changes little, because the papers are already shrinking without any help from AI. They cut our page count last year and stopped printing one title on Thursdays. AI flopping doesn't save a weekly paper that's already lost half its adverts to the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep covering the clubs and doing it the way I do. I'd probably keep an eye out for other jobs, maybe at the county football association or a club media role. Cut back on eating out after games, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, a bit on edge. Every time Clive says we need a chat, my stomach drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a club media role look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running the website and social media for one of the bigger clubs, maybe the town club. It's often part-time or unpaid, though, which is the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your plan if the papers cut you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't have one. I'd probably do coaching for the under-twelves, I've got the basic badge, and get some bar shifts at the rugby club.

say: I'd say I'm **glad** AI isn't taking over.
I'd say at the club bar you still need someone who knows the **keeper's** bad week.
think: The papers are **already shrinking**, AI or no AI.
Page counts were cut and one title **stopped printing** on Thursdays.
do: Keep covering clubs **by hand** as I always have.
Watch for jobs at the **county FA** or a club media role.
Cut back on **eating out** after games.
feel: A bit **on edge**, like now, whenever the editor wants a **chat**.
S0.quote: AI flopping doesn't save a weekly paper that's already lost half its adverts to the internet.
fieldNote: His fear predates AI: the papers are **losing adverts** and pages.
He has **no plan** beyond coaching and bar shifts, and admits it.
His world is **local clubs**, which gives him warmth but few exits.

steps.text: Keep writing match reports by hand for the three weekly papers
Check for openings at the county football association
Stop eating out after Saturday games

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame for local sport, because results paragraphs written by a machine have no feel. I'd probably keep it polite at work, though. I'm not one for making a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the results round-up is exactly the sort of writing the card is talking about. If the papers can get forty paragraphs out of a computer on a Monday, they don't need me for that. I think I'd go down to part-time or out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a bit to see what Clive does, because I don't want to jump too soon. But I'd start saying yes to the paid coaching sessions and the bar shifts. And I'd give up the car if I could, maybe share lifts with Dean (the rugby club photographer).

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Properly worried. I'm not good at change, and this is change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Clive asked you to learn the AI tool, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, because I'd have to. I'd be slow at it, and I'd probably make a mess of it at first. But I'd do it rather than lose the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the job do you think a machine couldn't do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Standing on the touchline when the old groundsman tells you the club's about to fold. A computer can write the score from the scoresheet, but the scoresheet doesn't tell you the club is about to lose its ground.

say: I'd say machine-written results have **no feel** for local sport.
I'd keep it **polite at work** and not make a fuss.
think: The Monday **results round-up** is exactly what the card describes.
I'd likely drop to **part-time** or be let go.
do: Wait to see what **Clive** decides before acting.
Say yes to paid **coaching sessions** and bar shifts.
Share lifts with **Dean** to get rid of the car.
feel: **Properly worried**, because he isn't good at **change**.
S1.quote: A computer can write the score from the scoresheet, but the scoresheet doesn't tell you the club is about to lose its ground.
fieldNote: He names the **results round-up** as the exact task the card takes.
He'd learn the tools only if **forced**, and expects to be slow.
His instinct is to **wait**, even while he lines up side shifts.

steps.text: Wait for the sports editor's decision before changing anything
Take paid under-twelves coaching sessions on weekday evenings
Share lifts to grounds and sell the car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and I'd say it plainly. I'd say the government needs to do something, though I wouldn't know what. I'd probably just talk about it at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be done as a reporter by 2028. No savings, no other skills that pay, no idea what to do. I'd panic, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my parents if I could move back into my old room, which is in a town with even fewer jobs. I'd pick up every shift going at the rugby club bar. I'd look at labouring or warehouse work, because the card says robots take longer for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Two years is nothing when you've got two hundred quid a month spare and no other skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says hands-on robots come about three years after the thinking AI. How does that land for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the bar and the coaching last a bit longer than the writing. Three years of pulling pints isn't a career, though. It's a waiting room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, probably. She'd tell me to come home and stop worrying. My dad would say he told me to be an electrician.

say: I'd say plainly it's **mad** and the **government** must act.
I'd mostly talk about it **at the club**, not online.
think: I'd be **done as a reporter** by 2028.
With **no savings** and no other paid skills, I'd have **no plan**.
do: Ask my parents about moving back into my **old room**.
Take every shift going at the **rugby club bar**.
feel: **Panicked**, with no money and no clear **next step**.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing when you've got two hundred quid a month spare and no other skills.
fieldNote: He sees the **robot gap** as a waiting room, not a plan.
His family is his only **safety net**, in a town with fewer jobs.
He offers no **policy** idea, just a sense that someone should act.

steps.text: Move back into his parents' spare room
Ask his parents for help while he finds work
Take every bar shift at the rugby club
Apply for labouring and warehouse jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort something out, and people should. At work I'd keep my head down. At the club I'd say the papers will be the first to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a bit of time to get out, but I'm not good at getting out. I'd probably stay too long. I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the next coaching badge this year, which costs a few hundred, and try to get paid work with a club academy. I'd start putting twenty a week aside. And I'd talk to my dad's mate about an electrician apprenticeship, even though I'd be the oldest one there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but less than the fast one. Five years is enough to see it coming and still not move, if you're someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stay too long. What would make you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Clive leaving, or the papers merging. If the person who hired me goes, I'll take that as the sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Coaching or electrician, which is more real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coaching is what I want; electrician is what pays. I'd probably try coaching first and regret not starting the other sooner.

say: I'd say there's **time to sort** something out.
At the club I'd say the **papers** will be the first to go.
think: Five years gives me **time to leave**, but I'm not good at leaving.
I'd probably **stay too long**, and I know it.
do: Do the next **coaching badge** this year for a few hundred.
Ask about an **electrician apprenticeship** through my dad's friend.
feel: **Scared**, though less than with the fast version.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to see it coming and still not move, if you're someone like me.
fieldNote: He's honest that he'd **stay too long**, waiting for a sign.
**Coaching** is the dream, the electrician trade is the realistic move.
His mood stays high because the **job loss** feels certain, just later.

steps.text: Pay for the next coaching badge this year
Save twenty pounds a week from his wages
Ask his dad's friend about an electrician apprenticeship
Stay at the papers until the sports editor leaves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots will happen. I'd not say much else. Most people at the club would forget about it in a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is the one where I've got a chance. I'd be thirty-seven. I could get my coaching badges done and maybe do an apprenticeship without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the sports pages for now, because I like them and nothing changes yet. I'd do one coaching badge a year. In about year three or four, I'd start an apprenticeship, probably as an electrician, because robots come late to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Worried, but in a way I can live with. With ten years I get to keep my Saturdays on the touchline for a while and still have time to learn a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Saturdays. Standing at a muddy ground with a cup of tea, knowing everyone's name. I'd miss that more than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you stay in sport?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coaching, maybe. If I can get to the level where a club academy pays me, that's still sport and still people.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** and lots will happen.
I'd expect people at the club to **forget about it** within a week.
think: Ten years is the one where I've **got a chance**.
At **thirty-seven** I could finish coaching badges and an apprenticeship.
do: Keep doing the **sports pages** for now.
Start an **electrician apprenticeship** around year three or four.
feel: **Worried**, but in a way he can **live with**.
S4.quote: With ten years I get to keep my Saturdays on the touchline for a while and still have time to learn a trade.
fieldNote: Ten years is the only version where he sees a **real chance**.
He'd miss the **Saturdays** more than the pay.
He uses the **robot delay** to pick a trade, not to stand still.

steps.text: Keep covering weekend football for the three papers
Complete one coaching badge each year
Start an electrician apprenticeship in year three or four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be out with nothing and no time. What would help is some money while you retrain, and an apprenticeship that takes people who are nearly thirty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the little clubs. If nobody writes about the darts league, the darts league stops feeling like it matters, and that's a whole pub's Tuesday night gone.

headlineQuote: If nobody writes about the darts league, the darts league stops feeling like it matters, and that's a whole pub's Tuesday night gone.
portrait: Umar is a **27-year-old** sports reporter for three shrinking **weekly papers**.
He rents a room, needs a car for grounds, and has a **couple of hundred** spare a month.
He has never used AI and **avoids change**, preferring to wait for a clear sign.
His fear grows with every scenario, from **page cuts** in AI Plateau to panic in the fast AGI one.
His exits are **coaching**, bar shifts, and an electrician apprenticeship, with family as a safety net.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be out of work with **nothing** and no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Money while retraining**, and apprenticeships that take people nearly thirty.
